Heterogeneous graphs

Source: vignettes/heterogeneous-graphs.Rmd
heterogeneous-graphs.Rmd
library(graphlearnR)

Many graphs have more than one kind of node and edge: authors write papers, drugs target proteins, users rate items. A heterogeneous graph keeps each node type with its own feature space and each relation with its own edges, so a model can learn relation specific transformations.

Building one

Node types are given as a named list; each entry is a feature matrix, a list with x, y, and masks, or just a node count for types without features. Relations are keyed "source__relation__target". Indices are 1-based within each type, so author__writes__paper edge (2, 3) means author 2 wrote paper 3.

hg <- hetero_graph_data(
  nodes = list(
    author = list(x = matrix(rnorm(8), 4, 2), y = factor(c("ml", "db", "ml", "db"))),
    paper = matrix(rnorm(15), 5, 3),
    venue = 2
  ),
  edges = list(
    author__writes__paper = rbind(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4), c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)),
    paper__cites__paper = rbind(c(2, 3, 5), c(1, 1, 4)),
    paper__published_in__venue = rbind(1:5, c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2))
  )
)
hg
#> <hetero_graph_data> 3 node types, 3 relations
#>   node author              4 nodes, 2 features, labeled
#>   node paper               5 nodes, 3 features
#>   node venue               2 nodes
#>   edge author__writes__paper: 5
#>   edge paper__cites__paper: 3
#>   edge paper__published_in__venue: 5
edge_types(hg)
#>                          key    src          rel   dst num_edges reverse
#> 1      author__writes__paper author       writes paper         5    <NA>
#> 2        paper__cites__paper  paper        cites paper         3    <NA>
#> 3 paper__published_in__venue  paper published_in venue         5    <NA>

Indices are checked against the size of their own node type, and the error names the relation and the side.

try(hetero_graph_data(nodes = list(a = diag(2), b = diag(3)),
                      edges = list(a__r__b = rbind(3, 1))))
#> Error : Invalid hetero_graph_data:
#> * Relation `a__r__b`: source indices must be in 1:2 (type `a`).

Reverse relations

Messages flow along edge direction. Without a reverse of author__writes__paper, papers would never send information to authors. add_reverse_relations() adds paper__rev_writes__author and records the pairing, which the link splitter uses to prevent leakage.

hg <- add_reverse_relations(hg)
edge_types(hg)[, c("key", "reverse")]
#>                              key                        reverse
#> 1          author__writes__paper      paper__rev_writes__author
#> 2            paper__cites__paper        paper__rev_cites__paper
#> 3     paper__published_in__venue venue__rev_published_in__paper
#> 4      paper__rev_writes__author          author__writes__paper
#> 5        paper__rev_cites__paper            paper__cites__paper
#> 6 venue__rev_published_in__paper     paper__published_in__venue

Homogeneous view

to_homogeneous() places every type in one index space with offsets, pads features to a common width, and records the original type of each node and edge. This is useful for exporting to tools that do not know about types.

flat <- to_homogeneous(hg, target_type = "author")
flat
#> <graph_data> directed graph: 11 nodes, 26 edges
#>   node features [11 x 3]
#>   node labels: factor with 2 levels
flat$metadata$type_ptr
#> author  paper  venue 
#>      0      4      9
table(flat$edge_type)
#> 
#>          author__writes__paper            paper__cites__paper 
#>                              5                              3 
#>     paper__published_in__venue      paper__rev_writes__author 
#>                              5                              5 
#>        paper__rev_cites__paper venue__rev_published_in__paper 
#>                              3                              5

A worked example: drug classes

dataset_synthetic_hetero() simulates drugs that target proteins and proteins that interact. A drug’s class is determined by the proteins it targets more than by its own features, so a model must pass messages across the relation.

dh <- add_reverse_relations(dataset_synthetic_hetero(seed = 1))
dh
#> <hetero_graph_data> 2 node types, 4 relations
#>   node drug               60 nodes, 4 features, labeled
#>   node protein            80 nodes, 6 features
#>   edge drug__targets__protein: 300
#>   edge protein__interacts__protein: 234
#>   edge protein__rev_targets__drug: 300
#>   edge protein__rev_interacts__protein: 234

hetero_gnn_model() builds one convolution per relation and per layer and sums (or averages) the results that arrive at each node type. Node types without features get a learned embedding.

library(torch)
results <- list()
for (cv in c("sage", "graph_conv", "gat", "rgcn", "hgt")) {
  torch_manual_seed(1)
  m <- hetero_gnn_model(dh, hidden_dim = 32, output_dim = 3, target_type = "drug",
                        conv = cv, dropout = 0.2)
  fit <- train_graph_model(m, dh, "node_classification", target_type = "drug",
                           epochs = 80, lr = 0.01, seed = 1)
  ev <- evaluate_graph_model(fit, dh)
  results[[cv]] <- ev$value[ev$metric == "accuracy"]
}
unlist(results)
#>       sage graph_conv        gat       rgcn        hgt 
#>       1.00       1.00       0.75       1.00       0.75

conv = "rgcn" shares bases across relations when num_bases is set, which helps when there are many relations with few edges each.

conv = "hgt" uses heterogeneous graph transformer layers (Hu et al. 2020), see hgt_conv(). Keys, queries and values are projected with weights per node type, each relation has its own attention and message matrices, and the attention softmax at a node runs over all its incoming edges across relations, so relations compete for attention.

layer <- hgt_conv(dh$node_types, names(dh$edges), 8, 8, heads = 2)
ht <- hetero_tensors(dh)
x <- list(drug = torch_randn(60, 8), protein = torch_randn(80, 8))
out <- layer(x, ht$edge_index)
lapply(out, dim)
#> $drug
#> [1] 60  8
#> 
#> $protein
#> [1] 80  8
a <- layer$last_attention$protein
summary(as.numeric(scatter_sum(a$alpha, a$index, 80)$sum(dim = 2)))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>       2       2       2       2       2       2

The last line sums the attention each protein gives to its neighbors per head; every protein with incoming edges gets exactly one per head, which is 2 here.

HGT also has the paper’s relative temporal encoding. Give each relation an edge_time, the time of the edge relative to its target (for example the citing paper’s year minus the cited paper’s), and set temporal_encoding = TRUE. A sinusoidal encoding of that time difference is projected and added to the source features before the keys and values are computed, so the same neighbor can count differently depending on how long ago the interaction was. Reverse relations get the negated times.

dt <- dataset_synthetic_hetero(seed = 1)
set.seed(1)
dt$edges$drug__targets__protein$edge_time <- runif(ncol(dt$edges$drug__targets__protein$edge_index), 0, 5)
dt <- add_reverse_relations(dt)
summary(dt$edges$protein__rev_targets__drug$edge_time)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#> -4.96342 -3.61857 -2.38733 -2.45056 -1.28959 -0.06539
torch_manual_seed(1)
m_rte <- hetero_gnn_model(dt, hidden_dim = 32, output_dim = 3, target_type = "drug",
                          conv = "hgt", temporal_encoding = TRUE, dropout = 0.2)
fit_rte <- train_graph_model(m_rte, dt, "node_classification", target_type = "drug",
                             epochs = 80, lr = 0.01, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_rte, dt)[1, ]
#>     metric value
#> 1 accuracy  0.75

Relations without edge_time use a time difference of zero.

Relation specific link prediction

split_edges_hetero() splits one relation. Held out edges are removed both from that relation and from its reverse, otherwise the model could read a test edge backwards during message passing. Negatives are drawn with the source from the source type and the target from the target type.

sp <- split_edges_hetero(dh, "drug__targets__protein", val = 0.1, test = 0.2, seed = 2)
sp
#> <hetero_link_split> drug__targets__protein: train 210, val 30 (+30 neg), test 60 (+60 neg)
held <- paste(sp$test_pos[1, ], sp$test_pos[2, ])
rev <- sp$train_graph$edges$protein__rev_targets__drug$edge_index
any(paste(rev[2, ], rev[1, ]) %in% held)
#> [1] FALSE
torch_manual_seed(2)
m <- hetero_gnn_model(dh, hidden_dim = 32, conv = "sage", dropout = 0)
fit_l <- train_graph_model(m, sp, "link_prediction", epochs = 60, seed = 2)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_l)
#>              metric      value
#> 1           roc_auc 0.53750000
#> 2 average_precision 0.55200494
#> 3               mrr 0.08820665
#> 4            hits@1 0.00000000
#> 5           hits@10 0.21666667
#> 6           hits@50 0.93333333

Typed neighbor sampling

sample_hetero_neighbors() samples incoming edges of every relation hop by hop, starting from seeds of one or more types. Fanouts can be one number per hop for all relations, or a named list per relation; a relation left out of the list is not sampled.

sg <- sample_hetero_neighbors(dh, seeds = list(drug = c(1, 2)), fanouts = c(3, 2),
                              seed = 1)
lengths(sg$n_id)
#>    drug protein 
#>      10      15
vapply(sg$edges, function(e) ncol(e$edge_index), integer(1))
#>          drug__targets__protein     protein__interacts__protein 
#>                              12                              10 
#>      protein__rev_targets__drug protein__rev_interacts__protein 
#>                               6                              10

Local indices map back through sg$n_id[[type]], just as in the homogeneous sampler.

Batching

hetero_batch() combines heterogeneous graphs with the same schema, offsetting indices separately for every node type and recording a batch vector per type.

hb <- hetero_batch(list(hg, hg))
num_nodes(hb)
#> author  paper  venue 
#>      8     10      4
hb$batch$author
#> [1] 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2
